utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. Mr. President, we would request that the Chamber, if possible, recess after the testimony of this current witness in order to allow members of our Defence team to interview the next witness, Nenad Krejic. We have been unable to accomplish that since your ruling that Dr. Karadzic couldn't interview him himself, we would like to be able to do that before he begins his testimony, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I hear from the Prosecution, could you tell us why the interviews were not organised earlier, i.e., yesterday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Yesterday afternoon we had already pre-organised a videolink interview with witness KDZ532 and so until 5.00 we were occupied, myself at the Detention Unit and Mr. Stevanovic in the videolink room, with that previously scheduled interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One further question. Is Mr. Karadzic's cross-examination of Mr. Krejic impossible without proofing him before his cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, of course not, Mr. President. Because if a witness refuses to consent to an interview, then we have to do the cross-examination anyway, so it's not impossible, but given that the witness consented, then we think that it's -- it's preferable at least that we have this interview and there shouldn't be any obstacles to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Obstacles is that we are losing time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We requested these interviews on the 1st of September and the 21st of October. The reason that they weren't accomplished is because the Registry didn't decide them until 7.59 p.m. on the 28th of October, and we filed an appeal first thing on Monday morning, you ruled yesterday, and so here we are. Sometimes those things happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you do still agree Mr. Karadzic can cross-examine him without proofing him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we don't agree to that, but we recognise that it's a physical possibility, but where a witness has consented to meet with the Defence, we think that he has a right to that before the witness actually testifies. But it's not physically impossible to do it because witnesses refuse testify -- I mean, refuse to be interviewed and we have to cross-examine them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. As Mr. Robinson just said, where a witness has consented to meet with the Defence -- and that's quite right, the Defence could have interviewed this person, as Your Honour observed, yesterday when you gave your ruling, that he may have been interviewed prior to their testimonies by one of the accused's legal associates or by the accused himself over the telephone. They've had the name since the 7th of May, 2009, and could have contacted and spoken to the witness before that. And in relation to even seeing the witness at 5.00 p.m. last night, that could have been arranged through the VWS, and it wasn't. And now we are in a situation where we have to -- there's the request for the delay, which the Prosecution thinks is unreasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could remind you that we started the week with a two-hour delay because the Prosecution wanted to proof a witness who came in late, so they could have also proofed that witness since May of 2009.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness wasn't proofed. That was the [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 9.12 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the Chamber has considered the submission as well as the Prosecution 's response and have come to a conclusion not to grant your request. The Chamber is not satisfied that Mr. Karadzic's cross-examination would not be possible without proofing the witness, not only in a general sense but also in this specific case, and the Chamber does not agree that the accused has an absolute right to proof a witness when the witness in question has agreed or consented to being proofed. While the Chamber finds it unfortunate that the Registry took so long a time in responding to your motion, if it is really necessary to proof the witness in question, i.e., Mr. Krejic, the Chamber observed that it could be done during the remainder of this -- of cross-examination of this incumbent witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll leave it at that. Let's bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't mean to prolong the discussion, but just to note that we just simply don't have anybody available to conduct that interview while the witness is -- this witness is testifying. So it's an ideal but not a practicality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And it occurs to me that by and large matters which arose - this is going back to my own experience, I must admit - by and large matters which would be raised in witness proofing can be dealt with in cross-examination. The advantage of witness proofing is it sometimes reduces the time for cross-examination, but its subject matter can be covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we are waiting for the witness, I'm noticing that the transcript is very rough this morning, and hopefully someone will listen to the tape and sort it all out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, I appear to be designated as a welsh man, "Morris Morris."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please be seated. We'll lift the curtain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll lift the curtain. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just two pages from the transcript before I show you some documents. On pages 59 and 62, what was put to you was Kupresanin's request asking for certain individuals to be pardoned. Do you agree that Kupresanin was never dismissed from any particular office, he remained an MP up until the very end except that the Krajina was abolished so he was no longer president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that indeed I never saw or met Mr. Kupresanin, but I know from the press that he did have some particular office in the R Krajina, but you know what, I was in quite a condition myself at the time and I was very busy, so I wasn't really following any of that. I know he was not dismissed. I never saw that in the newspapers or anywhere else in the media, something like that that he had been dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 65, I notice some figures, 4.403 detainees went through the camp, 2.900 were handed over to the Red Cross, 532 were transferred to Batkovic in order to be exchanged. There is a remainder of 328. Does that mean that persons were being released successively so that it was not only large-scale releases that took place but rather that every day a few people would be released if they met the necessary requirements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, until now it never crossed my mind to add up these figures. Now I see that perhaps I should have done that. According to our records, not the records of the ICRC, but our records, 4.403 persons passed through the camp. However, in the camp itself there were never that many people at the same time. It was always 500 or 600 less than that at one point in time, that is. Now, this is the reason: Prisoner exchanges took place all the time, two groups per week, so this was a flowing current, they were coming and going. The figure that you presented when adding all of this up and subtracting, it would seem that these persons were exchanged. Perhaps when groups went to third countries or something like that. At any rate, it has to do with an exchange of prisoners. Those who were transferred to Batkovic were also exchanged ultimately. Appropriate individuals and organs from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska assessed that we would need someone to exchange for our own people who had been taken prisoner, so that is why these individuals were transferred to Batkovic. 131 individuals were handed over to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps because they also had some of their own members that had been imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is why I'm asking this: The witnesses who were prisoners say here from time to time the names of five persons were called out and they never came back. This is something they state very often when they say they were taken out and never returned. When these groups or individuals were taken out, does that mean that they were killed, or if they never returned, does that mean that they were exchanged or released? Because the witnesses suggest that if they do not return, they probably get killed.

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I claim, and I abide by the oath that I took yesterday, that all of these persons who were taken out 5, 10, 15, even up to 40 individuals, that does not mean that the other prisoners would know what had happened to them. In most cases, it had to do with an exchange. None of them suffered or was killed, heaven forbid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at 65 ter 23506. If it's already in e-court, that is. But if -- oh, it is in e-court. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look. There is a translation as well, but could the Serbian version be zoomed in a bit. Do you agree that this is already the 13th of September, 1991, during the war in Croatia? This decision was taken, as it was deemed necessary, to organise a camp for prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: That's right. This is an order of the command of the 5th Corps. This is the time of the JNA, the 5th Corps had its headquarters in Banja Luka. This order was probably derived from an order from a higher command. That would be the SSNO or the 1st Army from Belgrade, to have the camp established, that is. This necessity was based on the fact that members of the ZNG who were fleeing from the Serb forces, or should I say the JNA forces, from Croatian Kostajnica. They fled across the bridge on the Una river. They fled into Bosanska Kostajnica. So they were enemy soldiers, at the time, if I can put it that way, they were armed, they were wearing uniforms, there were about 370 of them. I'm not sure how many of them there were, it's about 370 men who were taken prisoner at the time in Bosanska Kostajnica. And now, what could be done with them? A camp was to be established in order to carry a triage and to take all other security-related actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is also reference to the 3rd Geneva convention in paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page to see who actually signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was signed by then Colonel Talic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's a reference to Manjaca where food would be prepared and so on. Everything is taken care of; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. All of this is spelled out in very precise terms in the order. All the way down to logistical details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 400 meals per day and laundry and everything else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1846, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 65 ter 17847.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is the 7th of January, 1992? Again, it's still the JNA, and it's an order that has to do with Stara Gradiska and Manjaca, and yet again everything is prescribed as to what should be done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page. [In English] Ah, it could be -- it should be English. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you agree that it's the commander that is signing this, Lieutenant-General Vladimir Vukovic who was nothing in the Army of Republika Srpska but in the JNA rather; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: That's right. This is the month of January 1992. The JNA still existed at the time. For Bosnia-Herzegovina the JNA existed until the 20th of April, 1992. This is yet another order of the commander of the 5th Corps. It is still the JNA. The order has to do with the organisation of life and work in the camp, what they put there, Stara Gradiska. Before the war, Stara Gradiska was a prison, wasn't it. So it was being used now for prisoners of war, for keeping them there, interrogating them and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1847, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe it's a mistake in the transcript or perhaps you misspoke. Do you agree that the JNA existed until the 20th of May, 1992, not April? The JNA left Bosnia on the 19th of May? Don't you remember that on the 3rd of May they were attacked and then in Tuzla on the 15th of May they were attacked?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Possibly, it was a slip of the tongue. I know that it's the 19th or 20th. Now, whether it's April or May, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D425. Can we briefly take a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in this document Stojan Zupljanin is redistributing a telegram that he received from Dobro Planojevic, assistant minister for crime prevention on the 8th of June, 1992, and what is prescribed there is how prisoners of war should be treated, in the spirit of humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We also received similar orders through our own military chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D426, could we now have a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is again the 8th of June, 1992, and SRNA is carrying my appeal to the International Red Cross in relation to all of these paragraphs, and do you agree that this was a well known position of all the institutions there, to act in this way, that is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I said yesterday that from several levels and in different ways we received appeals and orders as regards the observance of the Geneva Conventions and the treatment of prisoners and detainees.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4724, could we have that now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Hasn't been released, Mr. Karadzic. It's not been released in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll go back to that later, then. 1D294, could we have that, please. 4724 was the previous one. 1D4274. I thought that this had been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It wasn't -- Your Honour, it wasn't a document that was notified either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see it in the notification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But the previous document that hasn't been released, 4724, 1D4724.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we are talking about 1D4274.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told it hasn't been released. Now we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Witness, that on the 12th of June, the Main Staff, and then it was modified to be resent from corps level, was an instruction issued on the treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page. In English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It specifies to whom it is sent, chief of security of the 1st Krajina Corps, and then it's sent on to Manjaca, what we see in handwriting, training-ground in Manjaca, the press service.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know that this was the position and this was sent to -- into the field?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That was the amended, or rather, adjusted order from the Main Staff and retyped. All the modifications that were done in hand were here neatly retyped and -- by professional typists and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1848, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D297 is the next document I would like to call up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree this is my order on the application of the rules of international laws of war that I issued as soon as I was elected on the 13th of May, but it was published only on the 13th of June, the day after that order by Mladic, and it was adopted by the same session of the Presidency? Do you agree this was done in keeping with the needs and requirements, but do you agree that it was not strictly necessary because every officer in our army was aware of this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I was not able to see this order for objective reasons, but of course I agree with the gist of it, with the contents, and I agree with what you said that every soldier in our army, and especially every officer, was aware of all this, even from their school textbooks, let alone after this series of additional orders and instructions and appeals issued before the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1849, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is ordered here, or rather, the minister of defence is authorised to issue instructions, et cetera. Could we now see 1D298.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is the instruction that the minister of defence was authorised to issue on the treatment of POWs, and here on page 1 we see 10 paragraphs and there are 19 more on the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Reed advises that this is P1134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we upload it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please. The Defence has a better copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this one has an English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see on page 2 here -- we now have two Serbian versions, we need one in English. We see it up to item 19 and then we also see a fragment of a capture card, and on the next page there is a supplement. Do you remember that you had documentation and forms to keep records on every captive?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, we used those forms but we also received it in the form of an Official Gazette, but we also had an instruction that was retyped containing all these items and all these forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is already an exhibit. We'll skip many documents that are already be exhibits and deal with the same subject. Could we now see D103.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is perhaps something you did not necessarily see because it was sent to Mladic, the minister of the interior, and the minister of justice, where I remind them that sometime earlier I had signed an official authorisation to the delegates of the ICRC and that it should be complied with because there were some incidents on the ground. So do you agree that the incidents on the ground were not due to the misconduct of these people but because of certain pathologies among the people on the ground and the general population?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't see this document. I wouldn't have been able to, but I agree with what is written here because we heard the same thing from the media, that pressures were great and that there were a lot of complaints against many camps and collection centres, and we felt the same in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 65 ter 17453.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One of the variants has been admitted into evidence but in this one the minister of health also joined in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17453.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's also the signature and the stamp of the minister of health. Would you please look at this. This is an instruction to all local civilian and police authorities without any restriction or date. What I'm invoking was issued in June 1992, and it says that the ICRC should be given everything they need, free access and free passage. Did you in Manjaca feel the effects of this? Did the ICRC come to visit pursuant to this instruction and other instructions to enable the ICRC to do their job?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. We did feel the effects of this, and I believe these missions of the ICRC brought with them and produced this paper or a similar paper and that was the beginning of regular and frequent visits to the camp of Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm there's no translation. I believe there must be one somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think second page of this document seems to be an English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page, please. My service has translated this. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do we have a date of this? You said it's June 1992, but I don't see any date on this document. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that Mr. Karadzic said there's he also the signature and the stamp of the minister of health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a hit confused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also have the version cosigned by the minister of health to strengthen this document. And as for the date, we did not put the date deliberately so that there could be no objections of expiry or something. Anyway, the agency SRNA on the 11th of July -- or rather, no, I'll tell you which document it is that we showed a moment ago. D426. We can see it was on the 8th of June, 1992. If necessary we can call it up, D426.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take your words. We'll admit 65 ter numbers 17453 as Exhibit D1850.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see 1D304.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe you were present, I don't know if we have this in Serbian, but I will be reading in English because the interpreters will do a better job than I. So on behalf of the Presidency, in fact, I was already president at that time, and I'm writing to Daniel Shiffer, and I'll read this in English: : [In English] "Mr. Shiffer, I wish to express my pleasure with you -- your and Mr. Viesel's visit to Yugoslavia and the Republika Srpska. In the circumstances in which the truth is distorted, the visit of persons of such a moral and humane authority as Viesel and his associates are in one of those rare -- is of those blessings -- of the rare blessings. "You have seen that Serbs in Bosnia have prisoners of war and that they are treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. The Muslim and the Croatian side do not respect the human rights of imprisoned Serbs. "So far the Serbs have made many unilateral gestures, including several cases of unilateral release of prisoners of war. The other side has not made a single reciprocal move. In spite of that, we are ready to make another move. In honour of Mr. Viesel's and his associates visit to Yugoslavia and the Republika Srpska and on the occasion of our Orthodox Christmas, we are willing to release all prisoners from Manjaca if the international community and the International Red Cross are ready to accept them and convey them to third countries. "We do hope and expect that Mr. Viesel's reputation of a man of high moral standards and respectability of his associates will exert pressure upon the Muslim and Croatian side to release thousands of captured Serbs." Do you remember the visits of Mr. Shiffer and Mr. Viesel to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, especially Mr. Shiffer, I believe he was there several times, and we even symbolically gave him the key of the Manjaca camp once it was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it ever happen, Witness, that any of the prisoners of war who were released or exchanged be captured again in battle and brought back to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. We did some research into that and I was surprised myself that people who had gone through what they had gone through and had the chance to go to third countries rejoined units on whatever side and get captured again. There were not many such cases but there were such cases, namely, that people who had been in Manjaca once were captured again and brought back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you believe it was reasonable on our part to request from the ICRC that prisoners be taken to third countries so that we don't end up reinforcing the enemy army when we release people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I also think that is reasonable and logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1851, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said you had practically on a daily basis and sometimes at regular intervals reports to the competent command; that is to say, the command of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 5775, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3724, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, then we won't dwell on this much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report saying that according to plan, two crews of reporters and cameramen visited and their names are listed. It's 8 August 1992. Do you remember the visit of these reporters?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: There were many visits by reporters, but I'd like to see the second page because if I wrote this then I must have been present when they visited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page. I believe this document has been shown before in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that this is signed by Radinkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be viewed in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It mentions that Kupresanin had been there at my request, or on my orders, and the president asked him to talk to commanders of pavilions, and two prisoners were released on that day, Ago Deronjic, son of Ragib, and Zuhdija Ramic, son of Dervis. Is this an instance of successive release of prisoners that you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Correct, that is a reference to the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you said earlier today, the people in the same facility did not necessarily know what happened with these people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: They usually didn't. What I'm saying that the other prisoners were not able to know and didn't know because there were many buildings. Some people were going out to work or volunteered to work, some were called out by name for labour duty, because when there were exchanges, the Muslim side would ask for specific persons, and if these persons happened to be in Manjaca, the names of these people would be called out and they would be released.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4556, please. But not to be broadcast. 1D4556. Can the Serbian version be zoomed in just a little for the benefit of the witness. This should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of August, a team of journalists appeared and then members of the government of the Serbian Republic of BH also visited to see the conditions of life of the detainees. They had an approval signed by the then prime minister, Mr. Djeric, and it says here that Colonel Vukovic also visited, and further on it says that he looked at the activities of the international committee of the Red Cross. Is this an authentic document? Does it reflect the truth? Were the visits indeed that frequent both by the journalists as well as the representatives of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Immediately after we received a large number of detainees who were transferred from Omarska. After that, visits were a bit more frequent than usually, but they were very frequent anyway. Everybody wanted to publish a bombastic piece of news, if I may put it that way. So this is a true reflection of the events that took place at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted as Exhibit D1852 under seal, but in the mean time, could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D4557 is the document that I would like to call up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The translation is still not in place because the telegram is not very legible, but I hope that we will be able to deal with it. Do you agree that here General Milovanovic, Chief of Staff, refers to an agreement that was signed by the minister of health in London, I suppose, together with the Red Cross and the government of the Republika Srpska about the compulsory submission of certain information about the prison, about the number of detainees and so on and so forth. This was drafted on the 23rd of August 1992. We were still in August in other words?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that we were also requested to provide certain information about the camp, about the number of detainees. I suppose that this was a reaction to these orders.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D1853, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D4558.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Two days later after Milovanovic's telegram, the command of the 1st Krajina Corps received something from you and forwarded it to the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I can see that in this document. Actually, it was the camp commander who provided the information. We prepared everything for him and he provided the information to the command, i.e., he first sent it to the assistant commander for logistics who sent it to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He received the telegram on the 23rd and already on the 24th he sent his reply and that reply was forwarded to the Main Staff on the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And here under 1 we can see that their names, the numbers, and it says here there are currently 3.659 prisoners, and we also submit the lists as requested in your telegram. However, in the note, do you agree that this commander denies the contents of the telegram in which he was criticised for not having allowed the International Red Cross to approach and that he insulted the team, the Supreme Command of the army, and so on and so forth? Do you agree that very often the complaints were not truthful and that I and the Main Staff at first understood them as being correct and that this situation resulted in discords between the camp commander and us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English there's another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he says that the Red Cross has visited the camp five times already.

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: The fact is that before the date on the document, there had been a few visits by the International Red Cross and journalists. I don't have a reason to doubt the note that was drafted and signed by the camp commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. Irrespective of the fact what people think of him and how they perceive him, he was very co-operative in terms of the visits of the Red Cross and journalists, and he wanted to be in the limelight. He wanted to have his photos taken by journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1854, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. If it is convenient, we'll take a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First break will be for 20 minutes and we'll resume at twenty to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I believe that you had very prompt and good communication with the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. What about the telephone and fax lines with Banja Luka, were they up and running at the time? There were no outages at the time, were there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: We used a military telephone line. The telephone line was up and running. We could communicate with Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about your communication with the eastern part of the Republika Srpska, Sarajevo and Pale, were those communication lines up and running or not? Were they compromised?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I did not need to use any such communications, but I know for a fact that those communications did not exist. There was a corridor between us so the lines were not up and running. I had a problem arriving from (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D4559.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the detainees did not willingly accept that they had participated in combat, i.e., that they were guilty of something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Witness. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, I'm wondering about a redaction, page 25, line 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From the words "from."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you answer, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question, if that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Do you agree that the detainees were not willingly admitting that they had participated in combat and do you agree that during our civil war, people were in combat in civilian clothes for a long time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as the first part of your question goes, it is in human nature to resort to all means to defend themselves, one of those means obviously is lying. They would say that they did not participate in combat, they did not carry arms, that they did not wear uniforms or that there were indicia to the contrary. And what was the second part of your question? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in our civil war people wore civilian clothes for a long time, that neighbours were fighting neighbours and they did not have uniforms? Also some people who were not combatants were sometimes seen wearing parts of military uniforms for various reasons, one of them being poverty? In other words, civilian clothes or a military coat did not actually identify a person as a soldier or a civilian, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Let's be economical. At the time, I agree fully that was indeed the case. Uniforms and civilian clothes did not mean much in our area in the last war. It was even perpetuous to wear civilian clothes, a track suit, or tennis shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document. This document was issued at Manjaca. I believe that it can be broadcast. It doesn't really matter. This is a letter from Manjaca to the 1st Krajina Corps intelligence and security branch. It says we hereby inform you that according to a record, we have 1.353 prisoners of war. Ramiz Grapkic was captured in Grapska. We interviewed 15 persons, statements were taken from 13 persons, and interviews are relative Kljuc. There is also reference to the attack on a military convoy which was planned and organised by Omar Filipovic, and it is also stated that 19 persons participated in that attack. Is that all correct? And you can also see their names; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the very beginning of Manjaca, an active officer or a commissioned officer was captured, and there were eight members of the JNA among them. There was the notorious Colonel Zarko among them. And as far as the convoy is concerned, after I arrived in Manjaca I learned about that attack on the convoy and the killing of five or perhaps six soldiers. Those soldiers were on their way back. They were still members of the JNA because the JNA still officially existed. I don't see what date this is. The soldiers were returning from Krajina or from Knin on buses. They came under attack, and I believe that the leader of that attack was the notorious Amir Avdic. He was an officer. He now holds an office in the Federation. He is still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page, please. Can we have the following page in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the top of this page, which you can see that Lieutenant Amir Avdic organised about 80 persons, of whom about 70 per cent were armed. They set out for Bihac, and it is estimated that in the territory of Kljuc municipality he was still hiding armed individuals, some of whom were on their way to Bihac. Would that be a customary report about the situation in the Manjaca detainee camp? There were daily reports and there were also collective reports, as it were; is that right? (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, you were right, there were daily reports that were drafted at the end of every day and then there were also periodical reports, and as needed at the request of a superior, there was also an overview of events that were previously reported. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1855, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4560, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was drafted on the 15th of June. This is a daily report which was sent to the command of 1st Krajina Corps to the intelligence security department. It says here that five prisoners of war were processed and thus new information was learned about the hostile activities of Muslim extremists in the municipalities of Kljuc and Sanski Most. Then notorious renegades are mentioned. They were -- they took to the woods and stayed there for a long time, and their names were Draganovic, Hukanovic. Hukanovic was a commander and he trained a unit consisting of 200 men. All those men -- men's names are mentioned in here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt again. Could we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. I wonder whether Mr. Karadzic should repeat his last question or you remember and can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could he please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. This is a daily report. Do you agree that in this daily report there is a reference to the processing of five prisoners of war and that new information was obtained about the participation of those names that are referred to herein in crimes, in attacks. There is a reference to Omer Filipovic, Asim Egerlic. There's also a reference to a "zolja" attack on a bus, that you will find this in the last paragraph. Do you agree that this provided enough grounds for those people to be captured, detained, and tried because they did whatever they did in the depth of the territory rather than on the front line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Not to go into too much detail, not to jeopardise my confidentiality as a witness, I can say that my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1856, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4561, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Witness, let me tell you why I'm asking you this. I would like to establish what were grounds for somebody's detention. Did you ever come across a situation where a person was detained because they were of a different ethnicity? Was that of the sole reason for their detention, or alternatively was there a suspicion that they had participated in a crime?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: At that time I did not think very much about religion or ethnicity. This was a less important thing in Manjaca. In Manjaca, there were a lot of Muslims, over 95 per cent of the detainees were Muslims. There were about 152 or 150 Croats, and there were five Serbs as well. Religion or ethnicity was not the decisive factor in the treatment, detention, or arrival at Manjaca. I don't know whether I have managed to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. I want to establish the grounds for detention. Whether it was justified or not. A pure suspicion that a crime was committed or that the crime was indeed committed or some other reason because in those municipalities from which the detainees hailed, 90 per cent of Muslims still remained living and were never brought to Manjaca; right? To be very clear, if there were 18.000 Muslims in Kljuc and only 1.100 or 1.200 were brought in, then I wouldn't say that religion was the main criterion based on which they were brought in, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I agree in principle but I cannot confirm the data that you've presented, and these are facts that are probably being taken into account. I don't know the pre-war population of Kljuc, and I also don't know which percentage came to Manjaca. For the sake of the truth, I have to say this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a daily report. Yet again what is being reported on is the processing of a certain number of prisoners, and then information is provided about new things that have been learned that either confirmed that someone did participate or refute that. So Azdemovic, Senad took part. Look, Jasminko [phoen], so on. Was that the purpose of this regular processing, to establish whether a crime had been committed or not, and did you provide information on a daily basis about the interviews conducted on that day? The processing of prisoners on a particular day, that is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: That is evident from this report. What was focused on, if I can put it that way, during those days, was to capture the perpetrators of the attack against military column who killed a few young conscripts who were just doing their military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who were going back home and who did not constitute any kind of threat; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1857, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4562, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a daily report, again dated the 18th of June, and it says that Merhamet, the representatives of the Muslim charity organisation Merhamet visited Manjaca, and then what is described here is the information obtained, who illegally transported weapons to Kljuc and then the names of the perpetrators are listed here. And it says these individuals confirmed our knowledge from earlier on that Arif Hukanovic from Vrhpolje, municipality of Sanski Most provided weapons in organised manner to Muslims in villages in Kljuc. And then further down it says: In connection with the visiting POWs, we would like to point out that between 10.45 and 12.45 the POWs were visited by Adil Mehic; Esad Bajric, imam; - so that is an imam, right? - Hajro Halilovic; and the lawyer Amir Djonlic, all of them from Banja Luka. They visited on behalf of Merhamet. Can we move on to the next page now. It doesn't really have to be broadcast. Do you remember that in addition to the Red Cross, the Muslim organisation Merhamet also came? See, it says that here, they visited all the pavilions, they personally got to see how they lived and worked there, and on page 2 you can see who all the persons that received them were. Do you remember all of this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, Merhamet was among the first organisations, if I can put it that way, to come and visit the prisoners in camp. They brought them some aid, some food, that is, and clothing and medicine. As a matter of fact, we even handed over some prisoners to them. For example, persons who were younger than 18 and who had not been charged with anything else. There were several visits. I think that they no longer took place once the ICRC visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What it says here is that prisoners freely presented their problems and they said that food was not good. Do you remember that Merhamet was allowed to bring in extra food? Did they actually do that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, the actual situation was presented to Merhamet. They established what the situation really was like as they talked to the detainees, and I cannot remember exactly the food that they brought in, but at any rate then allowed to bring food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who cooked the food in Manjaca? Who prepared it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: From an organisational point of view, Manjaca was officially called a POW camp and that is what it said at the entrance and that is what the stamp also said. POW camp Manjaca. It was an organisational unit of the 1st Krajina Corps and since it was an organisational unit of the 1st Krajina Corps, that means that from the point of view of logistics, it was part of that corps as well. Just like any other unit or any other brigade, our quartermasters would go to the Kozara barracks in Banja Luka every day to get provisions. So they would receive food rations, that is to say bread, meat, vegetables and so on, depending on the number of POWs there. Whether that was enough is a different matter altogether. Perhaps other questions will deal with that. At any rate, they shared the fate of the people and the army at that point in time. In that situation, when there was a blockade, when there was a lack of communication with the rest of Republika Srpska, they shared their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1858, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4563, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is also a daily report dated the 20th of June and that 51 prisoners of war from Kljuc and Sanski Most were dealt with either fully or partially, and you say or rather what is stated here is that more or less well known information was received, information already received by the public security stations. And now what does it say here, on the road from Bjelajci to Manjaca, Pejo Grgic, son of Ivo, died on the way and his mortal remains were transferred further on. He never got into the POW camp, did he?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. He died on the road. He was transferred as is stated here. He was not registered in the camp. Just like the persons we mentioned yesterday were not registered. Those who died in front of the camp or in trucks, so the camp did not register persons who were outside its perimeter and that is the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Judging by the name, does this seem to be a Croat?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Pejo Grgic, son of Ivo, is a Croat, and I think that there was Pejo's son or Ivo's brother who was also in the camp. At any rate, he is registered and was exchanged and went to a third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1859, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take at look at 5497. That's the 65 ter number. Let it not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I did not have any markings showing that it had already been admitted. Perhaps I wouldn't even spend any time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see the date here. You see who the signatory is. And what does it say? Filipovic, Omer was interviewed further on, and what they learned about is what happened in Kljuc and in the villages around Kljuc; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time did you know where the front lines were? Am I right if I say that the closest front lines, to Kljuc and Manjaca, that is, were on the Una river over there, or on the other hand towards Jajce; whereas, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor are deep into our territory?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is the area of the 1st Krajina Corps that I belonged to as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4564. Can we have that now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is stated here is that important things were realised in connection with the attack against the military column, and it says new information was obtained as to who the participants were and it was confirmed that this attack had been planned in advance, and that Amir Avdic and others carried out that attack. So there is no doubt about that. All of these prisoners independently confirmed the information you already had or expanded on the information that their interviewers already had; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1860, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D4565, can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the following day and it says that Merhamet visited again - the representatives of Merhamet, rather - and that they brought in a certain amount of food, medicine, footwear, clothing, and so on, and further on it says that they asked for a list of prisoners and then they were told to communicate with the corps command, and then it says that 10 POWs were interviewed and previous knowledge was confirmed. So when they talked to this man Salif [phoen], they came to realise that Salihovic was commander, company commander in the village of Velagici. The company had three what?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Platoons. The first platoon commander was Momin Derisevic [phoen], the second platoon commander was Telfik [phoen] Draganovic, and the third platoon commander was Ramiz Tecevic [phoen]. Do you remember that Velagici is close to Kljuc, deep into our territory, far away from any front line, and that there was fighting there and that even crimes were committed on both sides?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, what part of the three questions is the answer yes to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I'd like to say: Is it correct that within such a short span of time, Merhamet visited yet again and brought in 1.500 kilograms of food and medicine and clothing and so on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: That is what the report says and, yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that it was established through interviews with these prisoners that there was a company in Velagici consisting of three platoons and the names of the platoon commanders are listed here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: That is what the report says and that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is the same village of Velagici where that crime was committed by the Serbs, the one that was investigated and punished?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page. There's another report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 25th June, it concerns an exchange of 61 prisoners of war, 16 from Kljuc. That means you released 16 prisoners on this day, over 60 and under 18; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's also a reference to the death of a person called Zlatan. Is it one of the three natural deaths, deaths of natural causes?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the cases of death of natural causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that's part of the same exhibit. Yes, it is. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1861, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a query for Mr. Robinson. Was this witness proofed by the accused before he gives evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, speaking for myself, whether there could be a more summary way of tendering these kinds of reports. You could ask the witness to examine each of these documents and then could put a more general question and then tender them altogether. I wonder, there would be opposition to such treatment or tendering in such a manner. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have fairly consistently explored with the Defence various avenues for rendering the process more efficient and particularly in connection with admission of documents. At the moment, I don't see a problem with that. We're happy to look at it carefully, but I think it's something well worth considering and we take the -- we'll take the Trial Chamber's suggestion very seriously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would also join in that, and I would say that the session with this witness was entirely devoted to looking at documents, so we did our best on that score, but if there's some way to expedite their admission, it would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I would be ready now to give papers to the witness while we wait to see them in e-court so that he can confirm the authenticity of the documents, whereas the contents is self-explanatory. If that saves us some time, I agree. Did you mean that the witness should look through the documents during the break or now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I meant during the proofing. And then you can ask a question that would cover all the documents, and if necessary you can touch-up on specific details, if you so wish. Please consult Mr. Robinson as to the appropriate manner in which you tender your evidence. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I will try to speed it up until Mr. Robinson formulates his suggestion. Can we see 1D773.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I was told that it hasn't been yet released.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 832 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the fifth line from the top where it says that through this work and interviews new persons have been identified as involved. So did this kind of work constitute a basis for new arrests of perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: When an interview yields information indicating that some specific persons were involved or perpetrated crimes, of course their arrest is the next step. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this has already been admitted as Exhibit P3736 under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is 1D4566 also an exhibit? Can we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this report says in the first paragraph that indications have been confirmed and there is one wounded person who had been in treatment and then returned, and then another five or six seriously ill who could be neither useful nor a threat to anyone anymore, and a suggestion is made to release them from the camp? This says also that you are trying to eliminate the mistreatment of prisoners and any other misconduct. You also mention a brawl between prisoners, after which one of them was sent to hospital in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted now because all the requirements have been met and it hasn't been compromised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also see -- can we see 65 ter 5517. Since it's already an exhibit and I didn't know that, we won't be wasting time on it. Can we see 65 ter 836. Let's move on, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. My list is not updated. Can we see 65 ter 18845. 18845.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this. Is this the usual accompanying document sent when people are sent for further processing to Manjaca? It lists the charges against them.

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the standard document but it's insufficient for further detention, so we asked the station to provide also Official Notes which are a longer document with more details about the acts charged. But, yes, this is a standard document that accompanied persons sent to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you see the last paragraph, perhaps it would help you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. In Serbian too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says they are asking you to receive them and they will continue the operative work themselves. Was it standard procedure for policemen from the police station concerned to come to the camp and continue the investigation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. This makes things clearer. Their men come to continue their work and to draft new documents concerning persons investigated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1863, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll skip everything that's already been admitted. 65 ter 5566. Although perhaps this is already an exhibit. No, it is an exhibit so we don't need it. Can we look at 65 ter 17840.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this telegram dated 19 August. It says: "On the orders of the highest authorities of Republika Srpska, all public security stations that have transported prisoners of war to the Manjaca military camp shall immediately create a file on each prisoner ..." et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would it assist you if we were to take an early break now, in terms of preparing your documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was thinking about how we would manage to do that. I think without meeting the witness again it wouldn't be possible but in the future we could possibly prepare some kind of 92 ter summary of our own and use it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we then continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Until 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 5600, please. 5600.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are waiting for the Serbian version. On the 22nd of August there were daily activities, day in, day out. On the 22nd of August, the chief of the public security station Prijedor, Drljaca reports that on the 20th of August they acted on the request and that they carried out a selection of detainees; whereas, on the 20th of August, they replaced those who could leave Manjaca in Trnopolje. Do you agree that that was indeed the case and that was just one of the activities in the series of activities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: This is what I can see in the document. I don't have any reason to doubt the veracity of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1865, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 5603, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention. On the 23rd of August, the following day that is, Drljaca writes as follows: "We are hereby informing you that the required documentation concerning the prisoners of war who have been transferred from the Omarska investigation centre to the Manjaca prisoner of war camp was forwarded to the commander of the Manjaca prisoner of car camp today." This means that there was intense activity. Do you agree that Omarska was considered an investigation centre rather than a prisoner of war camp?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that but I know that there were different names used for Omarska and Keraterm such as collection centre or investigation centre, but I don't know what those words mean, nor was I ever there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you do agree that this is just part of the activities that were launched by the administration of the detention camp and was supported by the state leadership, the corps command, and Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, I understand it, and I believe that the papers did arrive after that date at Manjaca in reference to certain people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1866, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me just see how many more documents I have left on this subject. There are just two more. Let's just go through them quickly. 65 ter 5145, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that was drafted on the 27th of August and it is about the hand-over of documents, i.e., supplemented lists? The hand-over took place between various police officers? The public security station sent this to the military investigation organs at Manjaca. Is this a proper description of those organs? Did military investigation organs really exist at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I believe that -- I believe that they used the term very liberally. It doesn't reflect the reality of the situation, if they had in mind what existed up there. Let's not go into private session. I believe that this is a rather arbitrary term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, they may have considered the processing of prisoners of war investigation; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1867, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another document on the subject, 1D4567.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the crisis in Vecici? Unlike Siparoga [phoen], Vecici would not calm down. They wanted their civilians to be released, they wanted to continue fighting, and now in December people from Vecici, 11 people from Vecici were arrested and sent to the camp. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1868, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's go back to the conditions that prevailed in the camp. The next document I would like to call up is 1D4568.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt again, but the witness answered "I remember that," but what's he answering "I remember that" to? "Vecici would not calm down. They wanted their civilians to be released, they wanted to be -- continued fighting, and now in December people from Vecici, 11 people from Vecici were arrested and sent to the camp."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard the intervention by Ms. Sutherland, can you help us, Mr. Witness? Would you like to see the document again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for that. The document was not drafted by me. It speaks about the arrest of 12 people and their bringing in from Vecici to the camp. I remember their arrival and that's what I meant when I said that I remember. As for Vecici, Vecici was one of the strongholds where people put up resistance and inflicted quite a lot of losses to us. The villagers of that village, I

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) went to negotiate and after the negotiations he was ambushed and killed; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the essence of the matter. Colonel Stevilovic, Inspector Markovic, and two chance passengers were in the car, and just outside of Kotor Varos as you are looking down the road from Vecici, they were ambushed by some barricades, they slowed down, three of them were killed and one of them survived and he still lives today. He survived and was imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this enough for the document to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I take it, Ms. Sutherland is now satisfied. Let's proceed with this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page and then to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber whether this is true, that the detainees were examined? The first medical examination was carried out on the 11th of June, and the 3.964th patient was examined on the 23rd of August 1992.
