This means from the 11th of June to the 23rd of August there were 3.964 medical examinations carried out; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: That's right. This is a protocol which was maintained by the medical bodies. This describes the examinations of the detainees, they were registered, and this log-book was set up at the moment when the camp was set up and existed until its very end. To this very day, you can find this -- these log-books in our archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1869, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up 1D4562.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we are dealing with the conditions that prevailed in the Manjaca prisoner of -- prisoner of war camp, and we are dealing with the reports on the conditions that prevailed in the camp. Those are daily and periodical reports. This was drafted on the 18th of June, and again you can see that Merhamet arrived to visit. I believe that this has been admitted, that we have seen it already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, [Microphone not activated] today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the following one, 1D4565 has also been admitted. Can you please confirm that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D1861.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D4569.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a record of the hand-over of medical equipment and medicines that Merhamet brought to the camp on the 24th of June? Everything is registered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page. And then the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see who received the medical supplies and medicines. Could you please look at the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the page be rotated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here that the record of the medical supply was taken by Dr. Mehmed Derviskadic and nurse Bozana Pavljanin. Was Bozana Pavljanin an employee and was Dr. Mehmed Derviskadic a detainee who worked as a doctor in the camp? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Mehmed Derviskadic was a physician by profession, and he was used up there as a general practitioner in the camp. There was also Enes Sabanovic who was a physician. They were both professionals. They had good bedside manners, they were very humane, and they applied everything that they had learned at medical school and when they took the hypocrit's [as interpreted] oath. Nurse Bozana Pavljanin was up there at the time. The camp administration changed the -- there was also Aleksandra Bijelic who replaced Bozana Pavljanin from time to time. In any case the two doctors were there throughout the existence of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since the other participants in this trial don't know much about the names in the former Yugoslavia, can you confirm that the two physicians were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: The two physicians were detainees of Muslim ethnicity. In the text I can see the name Aleksic. If it means anything -- or rather in the transcript, I can see the name "Aleksic" but it was Aleksandra Bijelic. I don't know if that means anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the transcript it says that Aleksandra Bijelic would replace Bozana Pavljanin from time to time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This would be admitted as Exhibit D1870. And we'll take a break now for half an hour and resume at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Excellency. [Interpretation] May I have 1D45775 [as interpreted] briefly, and we can add it to the document that has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4575.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Witness, that this is a sequel to that protocol of systematic health examinations in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this include each and every diagnosis, and did those two Muslim doctors who were prisoners sign this document? You can see that, can you not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is a continuation. Lest there be any confusion regarding the number 8.000 something, some prisoners reported for medical examinations several times whereas others never asked for a medical examination. So this is the number of medical examinations that were carried out by the doctor, and the signatures are basically the signatures of the two doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page. Can we have a look at the last number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what is written here is 8064 -- no, 34. That's the last digit; right? You would be able to see it if we could zoom in. 8.033 and 8.034. That's right. So there were 8.034 medical examinations, and as you said a few moment ago, some persons were examined several times; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, D869 as MFI'd, should this be added to that, or should a new number be assigned altogether? There is a translation. Actually, we don't need an MFI, we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I followed. MFI D869. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic put to the witness an earlier protocol and because that didn't have an English translation that was MFI'd, and Mr. Karadzic wants to know whether we can -- whether he can add this to that exhibit or this gets a new exhibit number and it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it this is a separate document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and I think it should have a separate exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll give a new number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1871, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have a look at 65 ter 5612.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus your attention on this. Do you agree that this is a report on a discussion with the ICRC, that is to say between the representatives of the ICRC and the representatives of the 1st Krajina Corps command? Mr. Kalinic was there, he was health minister of the government Republika Srpska, then the prime minister of the autonomous Republic of Krajina, Erceg. Please take a look at this document. Then it says here that Mr. Germont insisted on the unambiguous implementation of the London agreement, and then it says what was discussed, and the Serbs asked for lists of detained Serbs in Tomislavgrad, Bugojno, et cetera. Can you see this document? And also what was discussed then was the disbanding of Manjaca, Trnopolje, and this is what was agreed upon and then that is actually what is written there, what was agreed upon. Actually, can we scroll down on the English side a bit.

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Throughout the existence of the camp for months there was mention of a disbanding of the camp in exchange of all for all. I remember this and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this say in paragraphs 5 and 6, that Kalinic, Minister Kalinic submitted a list of prisoners in the camp and number 6 says: "During the day, at his explicit wish, the chief monitor of implementation of the London Conference visited the Manjaca prisoner of war camp accompanied by Colonel Milutin Vukelic" who signed this. And then on the next page it says that a person was seriously wounded by his father before the war operations started and you took care of this person; right? Actually, it's the medical service that took care of this person; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1872.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 5625. Could we please have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the work conducted by the prisoners and you mentioned today that some of them volunteered. Did they like going out? Did they volunteer? Did they realise that they would get extra benefits on account of that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, prisoners were used for farm work basically, digging potatoes, chopping firewood, actually, for heating the camps so for themselves. (redacted) because there was no central heating. When people were assigned to leave camp in order to work, it was basically done by seeing who would volunteer. Usually, many more people would volunteer than were actually needed. Actually, being in confined quarters all day was not pleasant and people were relatively young and healthy and they wanted to get out. So basically it was people who volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here that Colonel Vukelic says that this is in accordance with the Geneva Conventions because what they would be doing has nothing to do with combat whatsoever; right? The second paragraph, not for purposes of war and the conduct of combat operations. You see what it says here: "The use of prisoners of war does not run counter to the provisions," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the transcript to finish. That's why I'm waiting. Of course I have an answer. Vukelic was assistant commander for moral guidance in the corps, and he's the one who would usually give his approval for this kind of thing. It would seem that somebody else had asked for this approval to have these persons used for some physical labour and then Vukelic approved of it. He would sign this kind of document. That is the way things worked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1873, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D4576.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. It's a report of the Red Cross. They are saying that in accordance with the agreement reached on the 6th of June, 1992, that was signed by Mr. Kalinic on my behalf, so delegates of the Red Cross were allowed access to POWs in Manjaca for the seventh time already. And it says here the ICRC avails itself of this opportunity to extend their thanks for the full co-operation extended to them during their visit. Is that what they said to you? Did they say when they saw you how grateful they were for this co-operation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, they came six times by this point in time. Every time -- or actually, not exactly every time. They wrote these work reports and sometimes they would submit copies even to us, to the corps command, probably more often. And they described the situation, as they say here, sometimes as a matter of courtesy and sometimes they extended their sincere thanks for this co-operation and so on. I usually did not attend these meetings. For the most part, was it the camp commander who would receive representatives of the International Red Cross Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please focus on paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have the appropriate page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next one where it says they would be informed about transfers and so and so forth. And then it says: "The ICRC welcomed this move as a confirmation of future readiness by top authorities in Banja Luka and the camp administration in Manjaca to fully abide by the 3rd and 4th Geneva Conventions." Is this an indication of the readiness of the authorities in Banja Luka because the AR Krajina was very strong at that point in time and also because Krajina had not had any contacts with Pale -- rather, there weren't any good communications, there weren't any proper communications running at the time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: This happened precisely at the time when there was this interruption in our communications, rather the corridor was sealed off so decisions had to be made at these local levels; in this case, at corps level. Also the local authorities had to make decisions. There were some telephone communications, but I cannot say anything about that. So what is written here is reality as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page, please. Number 7 in paragraph 7, so we need page 7 in the English original as well. Then it's the penultimate page in English, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that what is stated here, that 44 sick prisoners were evacuated from the Manjaca camp to Banja Luka airport under ICRC supervision, and then it says the ICRC would like to thank Commander Popovic and his associates for their excellent co-operation and help during the whole operation. And then further on it says -- it says that the situation has been stabilised to a certain extent and that Dr. Emir Kapitanovic [phoen], one of the physicians involved in the examinations, was released on the 16th of September, and then there are other references to health related needs. Does this correspond to things as they actually were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, this corresponds to the truth. Or rather, what happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1874, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then may I ask for your approval --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask for a redaction on page 57, line 13 at least on my LiveNote. There's a few words after the word "themselves."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a similar document. 1D4577. If the witness could look at it so we don't have to offer it as a bar table motion. Another visit and another extension of thanks. 1D4577.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Another report. It says again that the visits are made based on the agreement of 6 June signed by Dr. Kalinic in my name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 6. Or rather, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that they are thanking the commander and the military administration for their co-operation, and they say it's agreed that the visits would be made twice a month in future. And then we see a table of all that the ICRC had brought, food, shoes, et cetera. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, this is authentic and it is consistent with the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1875, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4578 is the next document I would like to look at dated 18 November, another report from the ICRC, just the first and the last pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report on the visit from the 5th to the 18th November, so they stayed for 13 days on this occasion; right? Look at this, the highlighted passage: Commander Popovic described his difficulties. One of his men died at Manjaca because he could not be transported to the hospital on time. Colonel Djikic, chief of the medical unit, should, in co-operation with the military command in Banja Luka, be contacted in order to find solutions. There's also a shortage of fuel. Winter is approaching fast. Do you know about this case when one employee died because he could not be taken to hospital on time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, these problems described by Popovic were real problems, existential problems, and that's why he was trying, also through the ICRC, to get some assistance, and that death really happened. I wasn't there but it was an NCO serving in the logistics. He had a stroke or perhaps a heart attack, and if he could have been transported to the hospital on time, maybe he would have lived. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last page refers to the evacuation of 700 prisoners, food supplies would be adjusted. There's a reference to the tonnes of food handed over. That's the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then I would kindly ask that this be admitted. Here we have a list of tonnes provided, and it says after the evacuation of 700 prisoners the quantity of food will be provided accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D1876. Mr. Karadzic, you will have about less than 15 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. I have to move to another subject. And with your leave, 1D4579 briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Daily report at the time of the visit by Mr. Viesel. Do you recall that Mr. Viesel was free to speak to anyone he wished in the absence of the guards and that he could stay as long as he wished? And he did stay as long as he wanted to. He wanted to tour one of the facilities and he did. It was decided that it would be the third pavilion and that's the one he toured. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, he was accommodated and he was free to contact the prisoners that he wished to interview and speak to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does Mr. Karadzic have the complete document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately no, I don't have the page with the signature. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1877, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Because my time is running out witness, I would appreciate it if you could help me to present to the Chamber one dramatic event in September 1993 in Banja Luka. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Of course I remember because in that mutiny I was one of the casualties that was on the 9th or the 10th of September, 1993. We called it Operation September 93 when parts of certain units abandoned the front line and came to Banja Luka to deal with the situation. Unfortunately, those events were never fully investigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, shall we delete the last part from line 24?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since this is in the transcript that's been admitted, I'd like to show you a document 65 ter 1763 to see whether this report on page 4 of this document is consistent with your vision, your opinion of that crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember it was simultaneous with the attack of the Croatian army against the Medak pocket which was a UNPA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that the attack on the Medak pocket was overshadowed by these events that affected me and many other people. So I can't say it happened exactly at the same time but, yes, to some extent it did. I don't know to what extent it was deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the previous page it says "report on the events in Banja Luka from 11 to 19th September -- 10 to 19 September." Let's find the line which begins with 10 September. "In the morning of 10 September, individuals wearing uniforms occupied the main cross-roads..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have lost the page now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why did we change the English page? Probably next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. From the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "In the morning of 10 September ..." Please read the Serbian version. Do you need it enlarged?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I believe we have now the wrong page in Serbian too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we should go one page back, to the previous one. No, the first thing that was shown, the top beginning with 10 September. This is not it. Page 4. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they did all this, they arrested everyone from the building of the corps command, disarmed them, occupied the Security Services Centre, took into custody the president of the municipality, the president of the SDS, other public officials, tried to take over the TV relay at Kozara, and the Crisis Staff of the 1st Krajina Corps appeared in public and soon afterwards changed its name to the Crisis Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, which had its own seal. It was named the Operation September 93. Do you agree it was a major crisis that threatened us with complete destruction?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I remember this. Everything happened as described here, and I was wondering to myself whether at this time of major crisis we really needed the added complication of internal conflicts within the army or the state leadership. Yes, it's exactly as written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this passage: "Operation September 93 ended on 17 September..." It also says that I, myself, led the action to put an end to this along with the highest representatives of the army, the Ministry of the Interior, the national security.

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: That's correct. But I have to stress that Banja Luka was blocked at the time and General Mladic was the first to come in. I don't know about your activities, but I was there very close to General Mladic when he managed to get the men to stop all that and go back to their combat assignments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document 17763 be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1878, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 13352.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, do you agree that this called for my engagement in those military matters in view of the danger that threatened to escalate?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Karadzic. I know that you were at the forward command post in Prnjavor, that was a forward command post of the 1st Krajina Corps. I know that you came to a facility near Banja Luka and that you tried to deal with the situation. I don't remember what facility that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please pay attention to my order to set up the staff. I say here that I will personally command the staff and the staff will comprise of the following: Myself, Milovanovic [as interpreted], Mladic, all the way up to Zupljanin, and then I also ordered to raise combat capabilities of police and military units. I ordered that I would be the only one to be able to order movements, that reports should be sent, and so on and so forth. Do you agree that that was necessary in order for the crisis to be brought to an end peacefully without any bloodshed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. Fortunately enough, no blood was shed. If blood had been shed, there would be no end to the whole crisis. Obviously you got involved to deal with the situation and the situation was dealt with as it was luckily enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that ever again, save for those seven or ten days, I took it upon myself to be in command at the tactical and operative level? Was that the one and only time, according to what you know, that I got involved in command duties?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I can't remember that that was the one and only time that that happened, but in my view it was only logical that the superior person which is the supreme commander, if there was a problem or an incident in lower units, could jump in and deal with the situation, so I don't deem this to have been a big mistake, but that's just me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit at Exhibit D1879. And, Mr. Karadzic, it's time for you to wrap up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that there's two documents that are contained in the B/C/S version that was uploaded in e-court. The document that's been shown to the witness, but there's also on page 2 and 3 in e-court another document which a different date on it, so I suggest that only this first page is tendered -- is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now show you 65 ter 32300.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date of the document is 15 September 1993. 15 September 1993. Could you please look at the document and tell me whether you agree that it says here that there was a conversation between myself and General Milovanovic. I was probably in Geneva attending negotiations. There was a reference to here that a similar thing happened on the 14th of September at Pale. That soldiers were shooting, that they were saying this is Banja Luka, and so on and so forth. Do you agree that that event indicated that the flame of rebellion could spread?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I can't answer positively to your question because I'm not familiar with the event. I'm also not familiar with the document so I can't say yes to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether if this witness is a proper witness to deal with that matter. It's time for you to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, instead of putting a question to you, I would like to express my gratitude to you for having been very strict and very consistent in your activities. You should be proud of that but the Republika Srpska should also be proud of what you did. Did you have a feeling at the time that your attitude which was precise, strict, and consistent was in favour of the Republika Srpska and that that was in keeping with the policies of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: KDZ163 [Continued]
utterances.text: I didn't do anything for my own sake. I did everything for the people, for the Republika Srpska. If a similar situation arose again, I believe that I would -- did everything in the same way. I don't think I was particularly heroic in what I did. I don't think that other people wouldn't do the same. But let me tell you this: Whatever I learned throughout life and at school, I tried to apply all of my knowledge in such specific circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I have a few more documents left, but I will try to tender them in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, did you suffer any pressure? Was any pressure put to you on the part of the state leadership or the military leadership? Did anybody try to coerce you into changing your position and actions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can this be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this brings my cross-examination to an end. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, sir, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of my colleagues and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home, but please wait until we draw the curtain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a short break for five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I wonder whether you would reconsider your decision concerning Mr. Krejic interview given that the net loss to the Tribunal would be about 26 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can finish the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But then we can't interview him because he would have started his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We gave a ruling that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I know. I'm asking you to reconsider that ruling given that you now know it's 26 minutes that's involved. That's not a very big loss of time, a lot less than what we may have thought when you made the ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just leave it. In the peculiar circumstances of this case at the moment, the Chamber agrees to adjourn for today. We'll rise and tomorrow 9.00.
